transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
NPR has confirmed that the victim of an alleged rape at Cornell University told police clearly
in 2024 that she was raped.
That contradicts a statement from local prosecutor Matthew Van Houten saying that the woman's
initial account of the incident described it as consensual, NPR's Brian Mann reports.
This is extremely problematic for Cornell University and for this local prosecutor Matthew
Van Houten, Thomas Giefer, the attorney representing the woman at the center of this case, has
confirmed to NPR that in 2024 she gave a very clear statement to Cornell campus police that
she was raped.
Her statement then read as follows, "I can say with a hundred percent confidence I was
raped."
Those were her words.
Giefer confirmed it to us.
Van Houten, by contrast, has been giving interviews saying the woman involved told police that
what happened to that frat party was, and I'm going to quote his words here, "voluntary,
unconscious, and consensual."
NPR's Brian Mann reporting.
Tennessee Republican Governor Bill Lee is calling for a third party review to determine
what caused yesterday's failed execution.
From member station WPLN, Mariana Bacchiao reports attorneys for Christa Pike say she's
still alive but in critical condition.
This marks the second time Governor Bill Lee has issued a moratorium to review the state's
execution protocols.
A 2022 review found that the drugs used had not been properly inspected, leading to an
overhaul of the system and a new lethal injection process.
This is a process that has been used over a hundred times in this country without this
outcome.
Lee is term limited and will likely not be governor when the investigation is complete.
The front runner for the governorship, U.S. Senator Marsha Blackburn has called for the
state to quote "bring back the electric chair."
For NPR News, I'm Mariana Bacchiao in Nashville.
Google put a satellite in orbit today that it hopes can pave the way for orbiting AI
data centers, and PR's John Ruich has more.
The device is about the size of a refrigerator, and on board it has four microchips designed
by Google that are already in data centers on Earth.
The satellite is part of a research project at Google called Suncatcher because the big
lure of putting data centers in space is the nearly unlimited supply of free energy from
the sun.
Google plans to run AI workloads through the chips, testing how they perform after the
stresses of launch and while being hit by space radiation.
They'll also gauge how hot the chips get and how well they can be cooled by radiator
panels without wind or water to help.
The eventual goal is to launch constellations of similar satellites that will process AI
workloads, communicate by laser link, and function as flying data centers in space.
And a note, Google is a financial supporter of NPR.
John Ruich, NPR News.
The Trump administration has proposed a change to the 1040 tax form that will require Americans
to disclose their citizenship.
Officials argue the goal is to prevent immigrants lacking permanent legal status from receiving
benefits.
Critics express privacy concerns.
This is NPR.
A bill aiming to ban the sale of Chinese cars in the U.S. stalled in the Senate.
Lawmakers departed until after the November midterm elections.
The bipartisan bill aims to prevent China's auto industry from gaining a foothold in the
U.S.
It gained renewed energy last week during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit with
President Trump, the lone holdout Kentucky Republican Senator Rand Paul argued the bill
could unfairly sweep in Mercedes-Benz.
A new federal plan for managing the Colorado River goes into effect today.
It'll force big cutbacks for three of the states that use its water.
Alex Hager from member station KJZZ reports those states are trying to figure out how
they'll bear the pain of those reductions.
Arizona is slated to take the biggest cuts under the new rules, but it's close to a
deal with California and Nevada to soften the blow.
State officials say it's hung up while they figure out which specific cities and farms
will use less water.
John Bergrin studies water policy at the nonprofit Western Resource Advocates.
That's the real challenge, because you're actually talking to people about using less
water and getting cuts.
Nevada's decision to sue the federal government over its new plan may have also slowed down
negotiations between the states.
Arizona's top water official says he's very optimistic about the deal, which must be signed
before January 1st.
For NPR News, I'm Alex Hager in Phoenix.
A Tokyo court has awarded legal protection for the human voice in a landmark case involving
a popular Japanese anime voice actor.
The court ruled that Kenjiro Titsuda's voice was used without permission on TikTok.
The decision marks Japan's first acknowledgment of voice rights.
I'm Rylan Barton.
This is NPR News from Washington.
Stay tuned for the following announcements and messages from our sponsors.

topics.text: NPR confirms Cornell rape victim told police clearly in 2024 she was raped, contradicting prosecutor
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee calls for third party review of failed execution of Christa Pike
Google launches satellite with AI microchips to test feasibility of orbiting data centers
Trump administration proposes requiring citizenship disclosure on 1040 tax forms
Bipartisan bill to ban Chinese cars in U.S. stalls in Senate until after elections
New federal Colorado River management plan goes into effect, forcing water cutbacks for three states
Tokyo court awards legal protection for voice of anime actor Kenjiro Tsuchida in landmark case
